32048-cottage-building-in-cob-pise-chalk:
Clough Williams-Ellis's Cottage Building in Cob, Pisé, Chalk and Clay, subtitled A Renaissance, in its second edition, revised and enlarged, of July 1920, with an introduction by J. St. Loe Strachey, argues that Britain can build the million new houses it needs at once from earth, not brick. The country faces a famine of building materials: ten thousand million bricks are wanted, yet brickyards turn out only some four thousand million a year.

Williams-Ellis says telling house-hunters to turn to stone quarries is mere derision, and that lime, cement, and timber are all short, with no coal meaning no quicklime and no cement. Readers get a practical revival of cob, pisé, chalk, and clay building, with the author's own experience of pisé at its center.
nasa-tm-19690006771-i-123-production-by-:
Vincent J. Sodd of the National Center for Radiological Health and James W. Blue of Lewis Research Center describe making iodine-123 in this 1969 memorandum. Iodine-123 had recently been recognized as the most ideal iodine radioisotope for low-exposure measurements inside the body. A cyclotron technique produced it in high purity.

The method bombards antimony-121 with alpha particles, knocking out two neutrons to form iodine-123. The introduction explains the production route. The report record adds procedures for isolating the iodine products. It also covers recovering the enriched target material for reuse. Reliable supply of this isotope supports medical imaging with lower patient radiation exposure.
